say: You give it a segment $[AB]$ and a number $n$. It cuts the segment into $n$ **equal parts** without measuring.
The key idea: parallel lines cut equal pieces off any two lines they cross. Step off equal pieces on a spare ray, then carry them across to $[AB]$ with parallels.

example.question: Divide the segment $[AB]$ into three equal parts, using only a compass and straight edge.

steps.title: Draw a spare ray
steps.say: From $A$, draw a ray at any angle to $[AB]$. Make it long enough to hold three equal steps.

lines.text: Any angle works. It only has to be a different direction from $[AB]$.

steps.title: Step off three equal arcs
steps.say: Set the compass to any small width. Put the point on $A$ and mark $C_1$ on the ray. Keep the width. Move to $C_1$ and mark $C_2$. Move to $C_2$ and mark $C_3$.

lines.text: Do not change the compass width between marks, so $|AC_1| = |C_1C_2| = |C_2C_3|$.

steps.title: Join the last mark to B

lines.text: This line is the one the others will be parallel to.

steps.title: Draw the parallels
steps.say: Copy the angle at $C_3$ up to $C_2$ and $C_1$ with the compass. Draw a line through $C_2$ parallel to $C_3B$, meeting $[AB]$ at $D_2$. Draw another through $C_1$, meeting $[AB]$ at $D_1$.

lines.text: Leave all arcs and lines on the page. They are the construction lines.

steps.title: State the result
steps.say: The parallels cut equal pieces on both lines, so the three pieces on $[AB]$ are equal.

say: You give it a triangle. It finds the **orthocentre**, the point where the three altitudes meet.
The key idea: an altitude is a line from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side. Draw two of them and where they cross is the orthocentre.

how.higher: It appeared on Paper 2 in 2019 as part (a) of a 25-mark question, a construction of its own worth a scale of 15 marks.

example.question: Construct the orthocentre of the triangle $ABC$.

steps.title: Altitude from C
steps.say: Put the compass point on $C$. Draw an arc that cuts $[AB]$ at two points. From each of those points, draw an arc below $[AB]$ with the same width. Join $C$ to where the arcs cross.

lines.text: This is Construction 3: a perpendicular to a line through a point not on it.

steps.title: Altitude from A
steps.say: Repeat from $A$ on the side $[BC]$. Extend $[BC]$ if the arcs cannot reach it. Join $A$ to where the arcs cross.

lines.text: Each altitude meets its side at $90^\circ$.

steps.title: Mark the crossing
steps.say: The two altitudes cross at one point. Label it $H$.

lines.text: Two correct altitudes that do not cross earn only part of the marks. Extend them until they meet.

steps.title: Check with the third
steps.say: Draw the altitude from $B$ to $[AC]$ in the same way. It should pass through $H$.

lines.text: If it misses $H$, one of the arcs was drawn with a changed compass width.

higher.tip: Draw each altitude fully. One correct altitude earns more than a vague sketch, and two correct altitudes earn more again.
Two altitudes are not enough on their own. They must meet, so extend them until they cross.

sources.quote: Two correct altitudes but not intersecting.

say: You give it a unit length. It builds segments of length $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}$ with a compass and straight edge.
The key idea: Pythagoras. A right angle with sides $1$ and $1$ has hypotenuse $\sqrt{2}$. Put $1$ against that, and the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{3}$.

example.question: Starting with a segment of length 1 unit, construct a segment of length $\sqrt{3}$ units. Show by calculation that its length is $\sqrt{3}$.

steps.title: Build the right angle
steps.say: Draw a line and mark $A$ and $B$ with $|AB| = 1$. Construct a perpendicular to $[AB]$ at $B$ (Construction 4). Mark $C$ on it with $|BC| = 1$.

lines.text: Use the compass to copy the unit length each time.

steps.title: Find the first hypotenuse
steps.say: Join $A$ to $C$. By Pythagoras, the square of $|AC|$ is the sum of the squares of the other two sides.

steps.title: Build the second right angle
steps.say: Construct a perpendicular to $[AC]$ at $C$. Mark $D$ on it with $|CD| = 1$. Join $A$ to $D$.

lines.text: The two sides of the new triangle are $|AC| = \sqrt{2}$ and $|CD| = 1$.

steps.title: Find the second hypotenuse
steps.say: Apply Pythagoras to the new triangle.

say: You give it a statement. It tells you whether $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ ("$P$ if and only if $Q$") is **true**, by checking both directions, or whether a **contradiction** shows it cannot hold.
The key idea: $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ means $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$. If either direction fails, the statement is false.

how.higher: It appeared on Paper 2 in 2022 and 2023, as 5-mark parts: deciding whether an "if and only if" statement is true, and finishing a proof by contradiction.

example.question: Prove that $2x + 3 = 11$ if and only if $x = 4$.

steps.title: Split into two directions
steps.say: "If and only if" has two parts. Prove each one on its own.

steps.title: State the conclusion
steps.say: Both directions hold, so the two statements are equivalent.

higher.tip: To show an "if and only if" statement is false, give one situation where it fails. A counterexample is enough justification.

higher.tip: Writing true or false with no reason earns only partial credit. Always add the justification.
